questions.html: Let $v_{1}, v_{2}, w$ be vectors in $\mathbf{R}^{3}$, and suppose that the matrix whose three columns are $v_{1}, v_{2}$, and $w$ has three pivots. Which of the following statements must be true? Clearly circle all that apply.

options.html: Every vector in $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ is a linear combination of $v_{1}, v_{2}$, and $w$.
$w$ is not a linear combination of $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$.
Every vector in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$ is a linear combination of $v_{1}$ and $w$.
Every vector in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$ is a linear combination of $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$.

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 30)

Since the matrix of v1, v2 and w is having three pivots we can say that the vectors v1, v2 and w are Linearly Independent.

A. Since v1, v2 and w are three LI vectors in R3, we can express any vector as linear combinations of these vectors, so this option is TRUE.

B.Since they are Linearly Independent w cannot be expressed as linear combination of any other vectors, so this option is TRUE.

C. since v1 and w are in R3 we cannot express them in R2

D. since v1 and v2 are in R3 we cannot express them in R2

questions.solution:

The answer is C.

$$

questions.html: Which of the following is/are linearly independent sets ?

options.html: $\left\{\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -5 \\ 3\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{array}\right]\right\}$
$\left\{\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 2\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right]\right\}$

$\left\{\left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ -6 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{l}2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{r}6 \\ -9 \\ 3 \\ -6\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}\right]\right\}$
$\left\{\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 6 \\ 2\end{array}\right]\right\}$

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 14)

Few concepts that could help: -

1. Set of vectors are said to be linearly dependent, when there is at least one vector which can be represented as linear combination of other vectors. 

2. If there are only two vectors in a set, we can check whether there is at least one which is multiple of another or not, if yes dependent else independent set.

3. set containing zero vector is always dependent since it is trivial that coefficients of other vectors can be zero.

4. In Rn, max no of vectors in a linearly independent set can be n only. So if we find there are more than n vectors in set containing vectors from Rn, then it is direct that particular set of vectors are linearly dependent.

 

Now let's look at the question,

Option A: - Here set contains only 2 vectors and clearly no one is multiple of each other. So set is linearly independent.

Option B: - vectors are from R2, and ther are 3 vectors. so directly dependent acc to point 4 given above.

Option C: - since it is a square matrix, you can find rank and decide when nothing strikes while solving, if rank is same as no of columns, then LI set or else dependent set. Here V3 =  (2/3) * V1. so set is dependent.

Option D: - since set contains zero vector, it is dependent set.

 

Hence option A is the answer

Option C : Check that third vector is 6/4 times the first vector . In some cases its not that easy to check at first glance . For that apply determinant/, RREF/ devise shortcuts :p . FALSE

Option D : Zero Vector ...  . FALSE . ​​​​​​​​​​

1: $\text{rank}(A) = m$ and $n > m$ (Infinitely Many)

Imagine 2 equations and 3 variables. The rank is 2.

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

2: $\text{rank}(A) = n$ (No Solution Case)

Imagine 3 equations and 2 variables ($m > n$). The rank is 2.

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$

3: $\text{rank}(A) = m$ (At Least One)

If the rank is $m$, it means your columns are powerful enough to "cover" the entire output space.

  • If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, you can reach any $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (exactly 1 way).

  • If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$, you can still reach any $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (infinitely many ways).

4: $\text{rank}(A) = m = n$ (Always One)

This is a square matrix with "full rank."

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \end{bmatrix}$$

questions.html: Which of the following statements are true?

options.html: Let $A$ be a $n \times m$ matrix with $n < m$. Then there is a nonzero solution $y$ with $Ay = 0$ only if $A$ has full row rank.
Let $A$ be a $n \times m$ matrix with $n>m$. There is a nonzero solution $y$ with $A y=0$.
The rank of a matrix is equal to the maximum number of linearly independent rows in the matrix.
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix. Suppose $A=B C$, where $B$ has size $n \times r$ and $C$ has size $r \times n$. The rank of $A$ is less than or equal to $r$.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 36)

A) Let $A$ be a $n \times m$ matrix with $n<m$. Then there is a nonzero solution $y$ with $A y=0$ only if $A$ has full row rank.

This statement is false. When $n<m$, the system $A y=0$ always has a nonzero solution regardless of the row rank of $A$. This follows from the dimension theorem: if $A$ is $n \times m$ with $n<m$, then the null space of $A$ has dimension at least $m-n>0$, meaning there must exist nonzero vectors $y$ such that $A y=0$.

B) Let $A$ be a $n \times m$ matrix with $n>m$. There is a nonzero solution $y$ with $A y=0$.

This statement is false. When $n>m$, the system $A y=0$ may or may not have a nonzero solution depending on the rank of $A$. If $A$ has full column rank (rank $=m$ ), then the null space has dimension $m-m=0$, meaning the only solution is $y=0$.

C) The rank of a matrix is equal to the maximum number of linearly independent rows in the matrix.

This statement is true. The rank of a matrix is defined as the dimension of the row space (or column space), which is precisely the maximum number of linearly independent rows in the matrix.

D) Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix. Suppose $A=B C$, where $B$ has size $n \times r$ and $C$ has size $r \times$ $n$. The rank of $A$ is less than or equal to $r$.

This statement is true. When $A=B C$, the rank of $A$ is constrained by the ranks of $B$ and $C$. Specifically, $\operatorname{rank}(A) \leq \min (\operatorname{rank}(B), \operatorname{rank}(C))$. Since $B$ has size $n \times r$ and $C$ has size $r \times n$, their ranks are at most $r$. Therefore, $\operatorname{rank}(A) \leq r$.

Therefore, statements $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are true.

Source solution 2 (score: 15)

(a) is wrong: If $A$ is all zeroes, then $A y=0$ for any vector $y$, and $A$ is clearly not full rank. -

(b) is wrong: Let the first $m$ rows of $A$ be identical to the $m \times m$ identity matrix, and let the remaining rows be all zero. Then there is no such nonzero solution $y$.

(c) is correct.

(d) is correct: The rank of $\mathrm{A}$ is the least such $\mathrm{r}$.

questions.html: Which of the following is/are $\mathbf{TRUE}$?

options.html: If $A$ and $B$ are $4 \times 4$ matrices such that $\operatorname{rank}(A B)=3$, then $\operatorname{rank}(B A)<4$.
If $A$ is a $5 \times 3$ matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(A)=2$, then for every vector $b \in \mathbb{R}^{5}$ the equation $A x=b$ will have at least one solution.
If $A$ is a $4 \times 7$ matrix, then $A$ and $A^{T}$ have the same rank.
Let $A$ and $B \neq 0$ be $2 \times 2$ matrices. If $A B=0$, then $A$ must be the zero matrix.

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 36)

Let's analyze each statement carefully:

Statement 1

If $\operatorname{rank}(A B)=3$, we know that:
1. $\operatorname{rank}(A B) \leq \min (\operatorname{rank}(A), \operatorname{rank}(B))$
2. So $3 \leq \min (\operatorname{rank}(A), \operatorname{rank}(B))$, which means both $\operatorname{rank}(A) \geq 3$ and $\operatorname{rank}(B) \geq$ $3$.

Since we're working with $4 \times 4$ matrices, the maximum possible rank is $4$.
So each matrix can have rank $3$ or $4$.

Now for $\operatorname{rank}(B A)$ :
If both $A$ and $B$ have rank $4$ , then $\operatorname{rank}(A B)$ would be $4$ , not $3$ as given.
So at least one of the matrices must have rank exactly $3$ (while the other could have rank $3$ or $4$).

When we consider $B A$, we still have $\operatorname{rank}(B A) \leq \min (\operatorname{rank}(B), \operatorname{rank}(A))$, which means $\operatorname{rank}(B A) \leq 3$ (since at least one matrix has rank $3$).

Therefore, $\operatorname{rank}(B A)<4$ is true.

Statement 1 is TRUE.

Statement 2

If $A$ is a $5 \times 3$ matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(A) = 2$, then for every vector $b \in \mathbb{R}^5$ the equation $Ax = b$ will have at least one solution.

Since $A$ is a $5 \times 3$ matrix, it maps from $\mathbb{R}^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^5$.

For the equation $Ax = b$ to have a solution, $b$ must be in the column space of $A$.

Since $\operatorname{rank}(A) = 2$, the column space of $A$ has dimension $2$, which is a proper subspace of $\mathbb{R}^5$.

Therefore, there exist vectors $b \in \mathbb{R}^5$ that are not in the column space of $A$, meaning $Ax = b$ has no solution for such $b$.

Statement 2 is FALSE.

Statement 3

If $A$ is a $4 \times 7$ matrix, then $A$ and $A^T$ have the same rank.

This is a fundamental property of matrices: a matrix and its transpose always have the same rank.

For any matrix $A$, $\operatorname{rank}(A) = \operatorname{rank}(A^T)$.

Statement 3 is TRUE.

Statement 4

Let $A$ and $B \neq 0$ be $2 \times 2$ matrices. If $AB = 0$, then $A$ must be the zero matrix.

This statement is false. If $AB = 0$, it does not necessarily mean $A = 0$.

For example, if: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

Then $AB = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = 0$, but $A \neq 0$.

Statement 4 is FALSE.

questions.html: Let $A$ be a $4 \times 4$  matrix with determinant $7$. Which of the following is/are TRUE ?

options.html: For some vector $\mathbf{b}$ the equation $A \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution.
For some vector $\mathbf{b}$ the equation $A \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has infinitely many solutions.
For some vector $\mathbf{b}$ the equation $A \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has no solution.
For all vectors $\mathbf{b}$ the equation $A \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has at least one solution.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 31)

Since Determinant of $A$ is $7$, that is, not $0$. Therefore, $A$ has all non-zero eigenvalue.

Since $A$ has all non-zero eigenvalues. Therefore, $A$ is a full rank Matrix.

Since $A$ is a matrix of $4$x$4$. Therefore $b$ will be in $R4$ and the columns of $A$ will span the complete space of $R4$.

So, $Ax = b$ must have a unique solution for all vectors in $R4$. It means that all $b$ can be derived from the linear combinations of the $4$ columns of $A$.

A) True. For all $b$, $Ax = b$ have exactly one solution. Therefore, for some $b$, it is also valid.

B) False. Since, nullity = $0$. Therefore, $Ax = b$ cannot have more than $1$ solution.

C) False. No solution not possible

D) True. Exactly one solution comes under Atleast one solution.

(c) False - see part (a)

(d) True - see part (a)

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 14)

(a) TRUE, since $\left(A^{-1}\right)^{T} A^{T}=\left(A A^{-1}\right)^{T}=I^{T}=I$.

(b) FALSE. Take $A=\left[\begin{array}{lll}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]$ and $B=\left[\begin{array}{lll}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right]$. Each has rank $2$ but $A B=$ $\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]$ has rank $1$.

(c) FALSE. Take $B=-A$.

(d) FALSE. Since the rank of $A$ is less than $n$, for some (most) vectors $\mathbf{b}$ there will be no solutions.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

False.

If rank(A) < n, then null(A) is nontrivial. For a given b:

  • If b ∉ Col(A), the system Ax = b has no solution.

  • If b ∈ Col(A), the system is consistent and has infinitely many solutions (since any solution x0 leads to x = x0 + z for all z in the nontrivial nullspace).

Counterexample: let A=(0000)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix} (rank 0). For b=(1,0)Tb=(1,0)^T, there’s no solution; for b=(0,0)Tb=(0,0)^T, there are infinitely many. Thus the statement “for any bb” is false.

    Solution: False. Suppose $x_{1}+x_{2}$ is an eigenvector for $A$, i.e., $A\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right)=\lambda_{3}\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right)$. Then,

    $$

    \Longrightarrow & \lambda_{1} x_{1}+\lambda_{2} x_{2}=\lambda_{3}\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right) \\
    \Longrightarrow & \left(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{3}\right) x_{1}+\left(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{3}\right) x_{2}=0,
    \end{aligned}

    $\lambda_{1} = \lambda_{3}$  and  $\lambda_{2} = \lambda_{3}$
    hence, $\lambda_{1} = \lambda_{2} = \lambda_{3}$.
    in this case also we can't find two different eigen values, so that's again a contradiction from the given information.

options.html: If a system $A x=b$ has more than one solution, then so does the system $A x=0$.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 29)

(a) If a system $A x=b$ has more than one solution, then so does the system $A x=0$. True. If $A x=A y=b$ and $x \neq y$, then $A(x-y)=0$.

(b) If $BC=BD$, then $C=D$. False. $B$ could be non-invertible.
ex: $BC = BD \Rightarrow B(C-D) = 0$
now we can think like this: $2$ cases possible, either $B = 0$ or $C - D = 0$.
but if we take $C-D = X$ then the above becomes $BX = 0$ and that's a system of linear equations that means either $X=0$ or $B$ has linearly dependent columns. so we can say the possibility $B=0$ is a subset of all the $B$ such that det(B) = $0$.

(c) If $A$ and $B$ are $n \times n$ matrices, then $(A+B)(A-B)=A^{2}-B^{2}$. False. This is only true if $A B=B A$.

(d) If $A$ is invertible and $r \neq 0$, then $(r A)^{-1}=r A^{-1}$. False. The real formula is $(r A)^{-1}=r^{-1} A^{-1}$.

Using the fact that $A$ is symmetric, we have $\mathbf{x} \cdot A \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}^{T} A \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{y}^{T} A^{T} \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}^{T} A \mathbf{x}=A \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}$.
